title: The Mantel Clock: Form and Purpose
body:
Specifications: A mantel clock is a clock made to sit on a shelf, mantelpiece, or table, with a case typically 20 to 40 centimetres tall and 15 to 30 centimetres wide. Unlike a bracket clock, it has no carrying handle and no wall bracket: it stands on its own feet on a flat surface. Most mantel clocks are spring-driven and run for seven or eight days on one winding.

Mechanism: A spring barrel drives the going train, and a short pendulum or a balance wheel regulates the escapement. The movement sits upright behind a dial, usually with a separate strike or chime train that sounds the hours.

Maintenance: Keep the clock level on its shelf, away from direct heat and sunlight, and wind it at the same time each week. Dust the case with a soft dry cloth and never move the clock while its pendulum is swinging.

Build and restoration guidance: A shelf clock case is built as a rectangular box with feet, a glazed front door, and a back door for winding access. Restoring one starts with checking the feet sit flat, the door closes square, and the movement seats level in the case.

Tools: Soft cloth, spirit level, winding key matched to the square arbor.

title: Tambour Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: A tambour mantel clock has a low, wide case whose top rises in a gentle arch or dome over the dial, often with scroll feet and side ornaments. Typical sizes are 25 to 35 centimetres wide and 20 to 28 centimetres tall. The arched top gives the style its name, from the French tambour, a drum shape.

Mechanism: Tambour clocks normally use a spring-driven movement with a short pendulum behind the dial. Many are time-only or hour-striking; chiming tambours add a chime train and rods or a gong behind the movement.

Maintenance: The arched top collects dust along its curve, so wipe it with a soft cloth following the curve. Keep the clock level, since a tilted tambour throws the short pendulum out of beat quickly.

Build and restoration guidance: The arch is formed by laminating thin wood over a former or by carving a shaped crest. When restoring, match the veneer grain across the arch and keep the dial opening perfectly round so the bezel seats evenly.

Tools: Soft cloth, spirit level, veneer glue, fine sandpaper.

import math
L = 0.20
T = 2 * math.pi * math.sqrt(L / 9.80665)

title: Steeple-Top Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: A steeple-top mantel clock has a case that rises to a pointed peak above the dial, like a church steeple, usually 30 to 45 centimetres tall. The pointed top is a decorative case shape only: the movement inside is an ordinary spring-driven mantel movement. The style was common in nineteenth-century American shelf clocks.

Mechanism: The movement is spring-driven with a short pendulum, and many steeple clocks strike the hour on a bell or gong. The tall case gives room for a slightly longer pendulum than a low tambour case allows.

Maintenance: Keep a steeple clock upright and level, and take care not to knock the pointed crest when dusting. Wind weekly and check that the pointed top has not worked loose from the case sides.

Build and restoration guidance: The steeple is built from mitred boards meeting at the peak, often with a turned finial. Restoration must keep the peak centred over the dial, or the clock looks lopsided on the shelf.

Tools: Soft cloth, spirit level, winding key, wood glue.

title: The Mantel Clock Dial and Hands
body:
Specifications: Mantel clock dials are usually round or arched, 12 to 18 centimetres across, with Roman numerals for the hours and Arabic minute marks around the edge. Hands are typically a spade or moon style for the hour and a matching minute hand; many dials carry a small seconds subsidiary dial or a painted scene in the arch.

Mechanism: The hour hand is carried on the hour wheel, which turns once per twelve hours, geared down 12 to 1 from the minute wheel. The minute hand turns once per hour on the centre arbor. The gearing between them is what makes the two hands keep their correct relative speed.

Maintenance: Never bend a hand to clear the dial; if a hand rubs, the hand collet or the dial seating is at fault. Clean a painted dial only with a dry soft brush, since water lifts old paint.

Build and restoration guidance: When refitting hands, set the minute hand to twelve and the hour hand exactly on an hour mark, then check the strike matches the hour shown before closing the door.

Tools: Hand puller, soft brush, tweezers.

title: The Mantel Going Barrel and Spring Drive
body:
Specifications: Almost all mantel clocks are driven by a coiled mainspring inside a toothed drum called the going barrel. A typical mantel mainspring is about 16 to 20 millimetres wide and delivers power for seven or eight days. The barrel turns slowly, once per several hours, and gears step that slow turn up to the fast escape wheel.

Mechanism: The barrel drives the centre wheel, which drives the third wheel, which drives the escape wheel. Each wheel-and-pinion pair multiplies the speed: for example, an 80-tooth wheel driving a 10-leaf pinion gives an 8 to 1 step-up. The full train ratio is the product of its steps.

Maintenance: A mainspring should only be handled with proper spring clamps, since a released spring can injure. If a clock stops shortly after winding, the spring may be broken or set, and a repairer should replace it.

Build and restoration guidance: When rebuilding a barrel, clean the barrel wall, fit a spring of the same width and strength as the original, and grease it lightly with mainspring grease before closing the barrel cap.

Tools: Mainspring winder, barrel clamps, mainspring grease, screwdrivers.

title: Eight-Day Mantel Movements
body:
Specifications: An eight-day mantel movement runs for eight days on one winding, so it is wound once a week with a day of reserve. The going barrel holds a longer mainspring than a thirty-hour movement, and the strike train usually shares the same weekly winding rhythm. Eight-day movements are the standard for quality mantel clocks.

Mechanism: The longer spring and a slower barrel turn give the extra days. The escapement and pendulum are the same as in shorter movements; only the barrel and the first gearing differ. Weekly winding keeps the spring in its strongest middle range, which helps timekeeping.

Maintenance: Wind once a week on the same day, turning the key steadily until resistance rises firmly, but never forcing it past the stop. A movement that runs only five or six days needs service, not harder winding.

Build and restoration guidance: When fitting a replacement spring for an eight-day movement, match the original length and strength: too strong a spring overdrives the escapement, too weak a spring shortens the run below a week.

Tools: Winding key, mainspring winder, notebook for winding day.

title: Short Pendulums in Mantel Movements
body:
Specifications: A mantel case only has room for a short pendulum, typically 12 to 25 centimetres long, against the roughly one metre of a longcase seconds pendulum. A 25-centimetre pendulum has a period of about one second, so it beats about twice per second and the clock ticks fast. Short pendulums are more sensitive to level and to wear than long ones.

Mechanism: The pendulum hangs from a suspension spring at the top of the movement and swings the anchor, which releases the escape wheel one tooth at a time. Period follows T equals two pi times the square root of length over gravity, with gravity 9.80665 metres per second squared.

Maintenance: Level the clock so the tick sounds even, with equal gaps between tick and tock. Adjust the rating nut under the bob: raising the bob shortens the pendulum and makes the clock run faster.

Build and restoration guidance: When replacing a suspension spring, match its thickness exactly: a thicker spring stiffens the swing and changes the rate. Hang the pendulum so it clears the case back and the chime rods.

Tools: Spirit level, rating-nut key, replacement suspension springs.

for L in (0.12, 0.20, 0.25):

title: Balance-Wheel Mantel Movements
body:
Specifications: Some mantel clocks, especially French styles, use a balance wheel instead of a pendulum. A balance wheel with a hairspring oscillates back and forth, so the clock keeps time in any position and does not need levelling. Typical balance mantel movements beat 18,000 vibrations per hour, or five per second.

Mechanism: The balance wheel rocks on its staff, and the hairspring returns it each way. A lever or cylinder escapement releases the escape wheel at each vibration. Because there is no pendulum, the movement can be shallow, which suits flat or ornamental cases.

Maintenance: Keep a balance clock away from magnets and strong shocks, which disturb the hairspring. If the balance does not swing freely, the pivots may be dry or the hairspring may be touching, and a repairer should inspect it.

Build and restoration guidance: When rebuilding a balance movement, the hairspring must sit flat and centred between its pins, and the balance must be poised so it does not favour one side. Test the beat on a timing machine before casing.

Tools: Timing machine, tweezers, balance poising tool, demagnetizer.

title: Hour Striking and the Count Wheel
body:
Specifications: An hour-striking mantel clock sounds the hour on a bell or gong: one blow at one o'clock, two at two, up to twelve at twelve. A count wheel, a disc with a series of slots of increasing depth, controls how many blows the strike train delivers before it locks again.

Mechanism: At the hour, the strike train is released and a hammer lifts and falls once per count-wheel step. The wheel advances one step per blow, and when the deep slot arrives the locking lever drops in and stops the train. The total blows in twelve hours are one plus two plus three up to twelve, which is seventy-eight.

Maintenance: If a clock strikes the wrong count, never force the hands: let it finish striking, then check the count wheel position and the hand setting together. A strike that runs on without stopping has a worn locking lever or a bent count-wheel tooth.

Build and restoration guidance: When reassembling a count-wheel strike, set the wheel so the locking lever falls into the deep slot at the end of the twelve-blow sequence, then test every hour from one to twelve in order.

Tools: Screwdrivers, tweezers, hammer spring gauge.

title: Westminster Chiming Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: A Westminster chiming mantel clock plays the Cambridge Quarters melody on four chime rods or tubes at each quarter hour, then strikes the hour. The melody uses four notes, traditionally tuned to the first four notes of the Big Ben chime sequence. Four rods give four pitches, and the barrel plays a different phrase at each quarter.

Mechanism: A chime barrel with pins lifts four hammers in sequence, one per rod. At the first quarter it plays four notes, at the half eight, at three-quarters twelve, and at the hour sixteen notes followed by the hour strike. A separate strike train sounds the hour count after the chime.

Maintenance: Chime rods must hang free and not touch the case back or each other, or the tone dulls. Dust the rods gently and check the hammer leathers: hardened leather makes a harsh click instead of a clear note.

Build and restoration guidance: When tuning rods, shorten a rod slightly to raise its pitch, and always tune the set together in the case, since the case affects the heard tone. Keep the chime barrel pins clean and lightly oiled.

Tools: Rod tuning file, soft cloth, hammer leather, oil pen.

per_day_notes = per_hour_notes * 24

title: French Ormolu Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: French ormolu mantel clocks of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries pair a fine movement with a gilt-bronze case: figures, scrolls, and foliage cast in bronze and gilded with a gold-mercury finish. Cases are typically 30 to 55 centimetres tall, and many use a balance-wheel movement with a white enamel dial and a silk-suspension pendulum where fitted.

Mechanism: The movement is usually a French round movement with a balance or a short pendulum, striking on a bell. The case is decorative rather than structural: the movement bolts to a back plate inside the bronze shell, so the shell carries no mechanical load.

Maintenance: Never polish ormolu with abrasive cleaners, which strip the gilding. Dust with a soft brush and clean only with a barely damp cloth. Keep the clock out of damp rooms, since bronze disease starts as green spots on neglected gilt.

Build and restoration guidance: Restoring ormolu means stabilizing loose mounts with reversible fixings and re-gilding only where the original gilt is lost, never over sound original gilt. A restorer records every replaced mount before touching the case.

Tools: Soft brush, barely damp cloth, tweezers, conservation notes.

title: Triple-Chime Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: A triple-chime mantel clock offers three quarter-hour melodies, usually Westminster, Whittington, and St Michael, chosen by a selector lever on the dial or the case side. Each melody needs its own set of chime rods or tubes: eight rods for the fuller melodies against four for Westminster alone, so the case is deeper than a single-chime clock.

Mechanism: The chime barrel carries three separate pin tracks, and the selector shifts the barrel sideways so only the chosen track meets the hammers. A silence lever lifts all hammers off the barrel for quiet hours. The hour strike follows the chime on a separate train.

Maintenance: Move the selector only when the clock is not chiming, since shifting mid-chime can bend pins or jam the barrel. If one melody sounds wrong while the others sound right, its track or its hammers are at fault, not the whole barrel.

Build and restoration guidance: When rebuilding a triple-chime barrel, map each track to its melody before removing any pin, and test all three melodies at all four quarters before casing. Tune the eight rods as one set, in the order of the longest melody.

Tools: Pin chart, rod tuning file, tweezers, oil pen.

title: Grande Sonnerie Mantel Clocks
body:
Specifications: A grande sonnerie mantel clock strikes the hour at every quarter: it sounds the full hour count at the hour and again at each quarter, with a short quarter chime between. A petite sonnerie, by contrast, strikes the hour only at the hour and plays only the quarters in between. Grande sonnerie needs a large power reserve and a robust strike train, since it strikes far more often than an ordinary clock.

Mechanism: The strike train is released at every quarter and the count wheel or rack sets the hour count each time. At the three-quarter mark of, say, three o'clock, the clock plays the quarter melody and then strikes three. The mechanism must also keep the chime and strike trains in step so the hour never disagrees with the hands.

Maintenance: Grande sonnerie clocks need winding on schedule without fail, since a run-down strike train mid-sequence can jam the count. If the clock strikes the wrong hour at a quarter, let it finish, then check the rack position before correcting the hands.

Build and restoration guidance: Rebuilding a grande sonnerie train means testing all ninety-six quarters of the day in order, not just the twelve hours. Wear in the strike barrel and the rack teeth shows first, because they work four times as often as in an hour-only clock.

Tools: Quarter test chart, rack gauge, oil pen, screwdrivers.

demo.code:
total = 0
for quarter in range(96):
    hour = (quarter // 4) % 12 + 1
    total += hour
print(f"quarters per day: 96")
print(f"hour strikes per day (grande sonnerie): {total}")
print(f"hour strikes per day (hour only): {sum(range(1, 13)) * 2}")
print(f"extra strikes from grande sonnerie: {total - sum(range(1, 13)) * 2}")

title: Calendar and Moonphase Mantel Complications
body:
Specifications: A calendar mantel clock shows the date, and often the day and month, on subsidiary dials or apertures driven from the movement. A moonphase complication shows the moon's age on a rotating disc painted with two moons, advancing one step per day behind a shaped aperture. A classic moonphase wheel has fifty-nine teeth, so it advances two moons in fifty-nine days, giving a mean lunation of twenty-nine and a half days.

Mechanism: The calendar work is a slow gear train from the hour wheel, stepping the date disc once at midnight. The moon disc advances by a finger on the twenty-four-hour wheel pushing one tooth per day. Because the true mean lunation is 29.53059 days, the fifty-nine-tooth wheel gains about one day of error every two and two-thirds years.

Maintenance: Never set a calendar clock backwards across midnight, since the date mechanism can jam or skip. Set the date by advancing the hands forward past midnight, and correct the moonphase against a known new moon date.

Build and restoration guidance: When rebuilding calendar work, check the midnight jump: the date must change cleanly within a few minutes of twelve, not drag across hours. Paint a replacement moon disc to match the original colours and star pattern before fitting.

Tools: Moon age table, tweezers, soft brush, oil pen.

wheel_days = 59 / 2
true_lunation = 29.53059
error_per_month = wheel_days - true_lunation
months_per_day_error = 1 / abs(error_per_month)
print(f"59-tooth moon wheel lunation: {wheel_days:.1f} days")
print(f"true mean lunation: {true_lunation} days")
print(f"error per lunation: {error_per_month:.5f} days")
print(f"one day of error after about {months_per_day_error:.1f} lunations")

title: Servicing and Oiling a Mantel Movement
body:
Specifications: A mantel movement should be cleaned and oiled every five to seven years. Old oil thickens into a gum that slows the train and wears the pivots, so a clock that runs but loses time steadily, or stops in one position, usually needs service rather than regulation. A full service strips the movement, cleans every part, re-bushes worn pivot holes, and re-oils with clock oil.

Mechanism: Oil sits in the small sink around each pivot hole and reduces friction between the steel pivot and the brass plate. Too much oil spreads onto the wheels and collects dust; too little lets the pivot cut into the plate and oval the hole. The escapement pallets and the balance or pendulum suspension need only the smallest drop, applied with a fine oiler.

Maintenance: Between services, keep the clock wound, level, and dust-free, and note the winding day and any rate change. Do not spray oil into a movement from outside: it reaches the wrong places and traps dirt.

Build and restoration guidance: A service bench needs a clean tray per wheel, pegwood for pivot holes, and a record of which bush was replaced and where. After reassembly, run the movement uncased for a week and log its daily rate before returning it to the case.

Tools: Clock oil, fine oilers, pegwood, bushing tool, cleaning solution, tweezers, rate log.

title: Beat Setting, Regulation, and Troubleshooting
body:
Specifications: A mantel clock is in beat when the tick and the tock are evenly spaced: the pendulum or balance spends the same time swinging each way. Beat error is the difference between the two intervals, and even a small error makes a short-pendulum mantel clock stop or lose time. Regulation is separate: it sets the rate by raising or lowering the pendulum bob, or by moving the balance regulator.

Mechanism: Beat is set by shifting the crutch or the escapement so the anchor releases symmetrically. Rate is set by the pendulum length, following the period law: a longer pendulum runs slower. Diagnose in order: level, beat, power, then rate, since adjusting rate before beat wastes the effort.

Maintenance: Listen first: an uneven tick-tock means beat, a steady but wrong rate means regulation, and a clock that stops at the same hand position each day means a mechanical obstruction or a bent tooth. Record the daily rate against a reference before turning any screw.

Build and restoration guidance: Build a test routine into every restoration: level the case, set the beat by ear and by timing, run for seven days, log the daily error, then regulate in small steps. A clock that gains or loses more than a minute a day after beat and power are correct needs pivot or escapement work, not more regulation.

Tools: Spirit level, timing machine or phone timer, rating-nut key, rate log, tweezers.

tick = 1.02
tock = 0.98
beat_error = abs(tick - tock) / ((tick + tock) / 2) * 100
mean = (tick + tock) / 2
print(f"tick interval: {tick} seconds")
print(f"tock interval: {tock} seconds")
print(f"mean interval: {mean:.2f} seconds")
